entries.meaning: To make something curve or lean the body over — and, figuratively, to relax a rule, to yield, or to force someone else to yield.
examples: Bend the wire into a circle before you solder it.
He bent the coat hanger into a hook and fished the keys out.
The ice storm has bent every sapling on the ridge.
She bends down to tie her shoes before every run.
I bent over to pick up the coin and my back locked up.
Bend your knees when you lift the box.
The road bends sharply just past the old mill.
The river bent west and disappeared into the trees.
Water has bent light this way since long before anyone measured it.
I have bent the rules for you once already.
The coach bent the curfew for the seniors.
Good editors bend the style guide when the sentence needs it.
He would not bend to pressure from the board.
In the end the city bent to the neighborhood's demands.
The union has bent on wages but not on hours.
She bent the whole department to her will inside a month.
You cannot bend a language to a rule it never had.
They bend over backwards for regular customers.
The landlord has bent over backwards to keep us.
He is bent on selling the farm no matter what we say.
They were bent on winning, whatever it cost them.

senses.head: Curve something, make it crooked
body: The core physical sense: force something straight into a curve or an angle. The participle bent doubles as an everyday adjective — a bent nail. (гнуть, сгибать, изгибать)
examples: Bend the wire into a circle before you solder it.
He bent the coat hanger into a hook and fished the keys out.
The ice storm has bent every sapling on the ridge.

senses.head: Bend down, bend over (lean the body)
body: Intransitive, about your own body, usually with down, over, or forward. (наклоняться, нагибаться)
examples: She bends down to tie her shoes before every run.
I bent over to pick up the coin and my back locked up.
Bend your knees when you lift the box.

senses.head: Follow a curved course
body: Intransitive, of a road, a river, a coastline, or light. Nothing is doing the bending — the thing simply runs in a curve. (изгибаться, поворачивать, делать изгиб)
examples: The road bends sharply just past the old mill.
The river bent west and disappeared into the trees.
Water has bent light this way since long before anyone measured it.

senses.head: Bend the rules
body: Stretch a rule without quite breaking it. A fixed collocation — bend the rules, bend the truth, bend a deadline. (обходить правила, делать поблажку)
examples: I have bent the rules for you once already.
The coach bent the curfew for the seniors.
Good editors bend the style guide when the sentence needs it.

senses.head: Bend to something — yield, give in
body: Figurative and intransitive, normally bend to pressure, a demand, or someone's will. (уступать, поддаваться, подчиняться)
examples: He would not bend to pressure from the board.
In the end the city bent to the neighborhood's demands.
The union has bent on wages but not on hours.

senses.head: Bend someone or something to your will
body: The transitive mirror of the sense above: you are the one doing the forcing. Slightly literary in tone. (подчинять своей воле, гнуть под себя)
examples: She bent the whole department to her will inside a month.
You cannot bend a language to a rule it never had.

senses.head: Bend over backwards
body: Idiom: go to extreme trouble to help or accommodate someone. Always in this exact shape. (из кожи вон лезть, делать всё возможное)
examples: They bend over backwards for regular customers.
The landlord has bent over backwards to keep us.

senses.head: Be bent on something — determined
body: The participle used as a predicate adjective with on. It never means physically curved here, and there is no active verb behind it. (твёрдо намеренный, одержимый (какой-л. целью))
examples: He is bent on selling the farm no matter what we say.
They were bent on winning, whatever it cost them.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: Bent does double duty as an everyday adjective: a bent nail, bent out of shape, bent on winning. Same spelling, same sound, different job in the sentence. There is no ✗ bended — the only place that survives is the fixed phrase on bended knee.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic throughout, whether you curve the wire, lean over, or stretch a rule. No linking use; be bent on winning is the participle as a predicate adjective, not a copular bend.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive when you do the curving (bend the wire, bend the rules, bend the department to her will), intransitive when you or the road do the bending (she bends down, the road bends, he would not bend to pressure).
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — the coat hanger was bent into a hook, the curfew was bent for the seniors. No passive of the intransitive uses: ✗ down was bent by her, ✗ the road is bent past the mill (in that reading).

entries.meaning: To mix things into a single smooth or harmonious whole, or to merge so completely that the parts stop being distinguishable.
examples: Blend the butter and the sugar until the mixture is smooth.
She blended three paint colors on a scrap of cardboard.
I have blended this soup twice and it is still lumpy.
Their two accents have blended into something nobody can place.
The suburbs blend into one another for thirty miles along that highway.
By the second month the new hires had blended into the team completely.
This roaster blends beans from three countries.
The distillery blended eleven barrels before bottling.
New siding helps the addition blend in with the old house.
He dressed down so he would blend in with the crowd.
The gray paint blended in so well we walked past the door twice.

senses.head: Mix into a smooth whole
body: The everyday cooking and mixing sense. In modern American English the past and participle are blended; the old blent survives only in poetry and hymn texts. (смешивать, размешивать, взбивать)
examples: Blend the butter and the sugar until the mixture is smooth.
She blended three paint colors on a scrap of cardboard.
I have blended this soup twice and it is still lumpy.

senses.head: Merge, become indistinguishable
body: Intransitive and usually figurative: two things run together until you cannot tell where one ends. (сливаться, смешиваться воедино)
examples: Their two accents have blended into something nobody can place.
The suburbs blend into one another for thirty miles along that highway.
By the second month the new hires had blended into the team completely.

senses.head: Combine varieties (coffee, whiskey, tea)
body: A trade sense: mix different lots or origins to get a consistent product. This is where the noun a blend comes from. (купажировать, составлять смесь)
examples: This roaster blends beans from three countries.
The distillery blended eleven barrels before bottling.

senses.head: Blend in — go unnoticed, match the surroundings
body: Phrasal, about people trying not to stand out or about a thing matching what is around it. (сливаться с окружением, не выделяться)
examples: New siding helps the addition blend in with the old house.
He dressed down so he would blend in with the crowd.
The gray paint blended in so well we walked past the door twice.

entries.register: everyday — ordinary kitchen and conversational English; blend in is said constantly
entries.pattern: -nd — -nt — -nt historically; regular -ed in modern American English
entries.contrast: The spreadsheet lists blent because blend once belonged to this group, but in American English today it is a plain regular verb: blended, have blended. Blent now turns up only in poetry and hymn texts. Write blended. Watch the spelling too — blend is not bend with an extra letter; the two verbs are unrelated.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in every sense, from mixing batter to a newcomer disappearing into a crowd.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive when you do the mixing (blend the butter and the sugar, the distillery blended eleven barrels), intransitive when things merge on their own or someone blends in (their accents have blended, he blended in with the crowd).
entries.passive: yes in the transitive senses — the paint was blended on a scrap of cardboard, eleven barrels were blended before bottling. No passive of blend in or the merging sense: ✗ the crowd was blended in with by him.

entries.meaning: To make something by putting parts together — a house, a business, a case, a reputation — or, intransitively, to grow steadily stronger.
examples: They build about forty houses a year.
My grandfather built this table by hand.
The district has built three new schools since 2020.
She builds her arguments one fact at a time.
He has built a law practice out of nothing.
Two decades of steady work built that reputation.
Pressure builds along that fault for decades at a time.
The tension built through the entire third act.
By noon the heat had built to something dangerous.
The sequel builds on everything the first film set up.
The whole case was built on a single witness.
Later research has built on her 1994 paper.
Build a little slack into the schedule.
Congress had built a sunset clause into the law.
The cabinets are built into the wall and do not come with the house.
Salt builds up on the sidewalk all winter.
She built up her savings for two years before quitting.
The press had built him up as unbeatable, which made the loss worse.
He is built like a linebacker.
She was built for distance, not for sprints.

senses.head: Construct, put up
body: The literal sense: assemble physical parts into a structure or an object. (строить, возводить, сооружать)
examples: They build about forty houses a year.
My grandfather built this table by hand.
The district has built three new schools since 2020.

senses.head: Develop something over time
body: Figurative but extremely common: a career, a business, a case, a reputation, a relationship. The object is abstract and the work is gradual. (создавать, выстраивать, наращивать)
examples: She builds her arguments one fact at a time.
He has built a law practice out of nothing.
Two decades of steady work built that reputation.

senses.head: Grow, intensify
body: Intransitive, with no object at all: pressure, tension, momentum, or a storm increases on its own. (нарастать, усиливаться, накапливаться)
examples: Pressure builds along that fault for decades at a time.
The tension built through the entire third act.
By noon the heat had built to something dangerous.

senses.head: Build on / build upon — use as a foundation
body: Take something already there and extend it. Very common in the passive: built on. (основываться на, развивать (начатое))
examples: The sequel builds on everything the first film set up.
The whole case was built on a single witness.
Later research has built on her 1994 paper.

senses.head: Build in / build into — include from the start
body: Make something a permanent, non-removable part of a design, a schedule, or an agreement. (встраивать, закладывать (в конструкцию, в договор))
examples: Build a little slack into the schedule.
Congress had built a sunset clause into the law.
The cabinets are built into the wall and do not come with the house.

senses.head: Build up — accumulate, strengthen, or hype
body: Three related phrasal uses: a substance collects, a person gains strength, or the press talks someone up in advance. (накапливать(ся), укреплять; расхваливать заранее)
examples: Salt builds up on the sidewalk all winter.
She built up her savings for two years before quitting.
The press had built him up as unbeatable, which made the loss worse.

senses.head: Be built — of a person's physique
body: Passive only, describing body type. There is no active verb behind it — you cannot say ✗ He builds like a linebacker. (быть сложенным (о телосложении))
examples: He is built like a linebacker.
She was built for distance, not for sprints.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.third person: builds · -ing form: building (also the noun a building)
entries.contrast: ✗ builded is not English. And because built covers both slots, We built it and We have built it use the same word — the difference lives entirely in have. Note the vowel: build rhymes with filled, not with wild; the u is silent.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, whether the object is a house, a career, or a case. Never linking and never stative; it always names work or growth over time.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive in the constructing and developing senses (they build forty houses a year, she builds her arguments one fact at a time), intransitive when something grows on its own (pressure builds, the tension built through the third act).
entries.passive: yes, and very common — the whole case was built on a single witness, the cabinets are built into the wall. Note the physique sense is passive-only, with no active behind it: he is built like a linebacker but ✗ he builds like a linebacker.
entries.phrasal verbs: build in · build into · build on · build up

entries.meaning: To cover a surface with a thin layer of gold, or figuratively to put an attractive finish on something ordinary.
examples: Craftsmen gild the capitol dome about every fifty years.
The restorers gilded the picture frame last spring.
Someone has gilded the lettering above the door.
A third adjective just gilds the lily.
The brochure gilded a very ordinary roadside hotel.
Memoirists have gilded that decade past recognition.

senses.head: Cover with gold leaf
body: The literal craft sense — domes, frames, lettering, book edges. Gilded is the ordinary American past and participle; gilt has narrowed to an adjective before a noun. (золотить, покрывать позолотой)
examples: Craftsmen gild the capitol dome about every fifty years.
The restorers gilded the picture frame last spring.
Someone has gilded the lettering above the door.

senses.head: Make something look better than it is
body: Figurative and mildly disapproving, most often in the idiom gild the lily — decorate something already fine. The adjective gilded also labels a shiny surface over something less pleasant, as in the Gilded Age. (приукрашивать, наводить внешний лоск)
examples: A third adjective just gilds the lily.
The brochure gilded a very ordinary roadside hotel.
Memoirists have gilded that decade past recognition.

entries.register: rare — a narrow craft verb; most Americans meet it only in gild the lily and the Gilded Age
entries.pattern: -ld — -lt — -lt historically; gilded is the ordinary American past and participle
entries.third person: gilds · -ing form: gilding (also a noun: the gilding flaked off)
entries.contrast: Both forms are listed in American dictionaries, but gilded is what edited American prose uses for the verb — they gilded the dome, the age was gilded. Gilt has narrowed to an adjective in front of a noun (a gilt frame, gilt-edged bonds) and to a noun for the gold layer itself. Separately, do not confuse gild with guild — same pronunciation /ɡɪld/, but a guild is a trade association.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: applying gold leaf, or putting a flattering finish on something ordinary. The adjective gilded (the Gilded Age) is the participle, not a separate class.
entries.transitivity: transitive in both senses, and the object is obligatory — gild the dome, gild the lily. ✗ Craftsmen gild every fifty years needs its object.
entries.passive: yes — the capitol dome is gilded about every fifty years, a very ordinary hotel was gilded by the brochure. The perfect passive is ordinary too: the lettering has been gilded.

entries.meaning: To fasten a belt around something, and by extension to brace yourself for something hard.
examples: Retailers gird for the holidays as early as September.
The mayor girded for a long budget fight.
Hospitals have girded for flu season since August.
Gird your loins — the auditors arrive Monday.
He girded his loins and knocked on the director's door.
He girds his waist with a wide leather belt.
Stone walls had girded the town since the twelfth century.
The old atlas describes the island as girt by coral.

senses.head: Gird for something — brace, prepare
body: The only sense in ordinary modern American use, almost always gird for or gird oneself for. Slightly elevated in register — you meet it in news writing more than in speech. (готовиться, собираться с силами (перед трудным))
examples: Retailers gird for the holidays as early as September.
The mayor girded for a long budget fight.
Hospitals have girded for flu season since August.

senses.head: Gird your loins
body: A fixed biblical phrase, now used half in earnest and half as a joke before an unpleasant task. (препоясать чресла; собраться с духом)
examples: Gird your loins — the auditors arrive Monday.
He girded his loins and knocked on the director's door.

senses.head: Belt, encircle, surround
body: The literal sense of putting on a belt, and its literary or nautical extension to something ringed by water or walls. This is where the short form girt still lives. (опоясывать, окружать)
examples: He girds his waist with a wide leather belt.
Stone walls had girded the town since the twelfth century.
The old atlas describes the island as girt by coral.

entries.register: rare — elevated and mostly journalistic; alive in gird for and the biblical gird your loins
entries.pattern: -rd — -rt — -rt historically; girded is the usual American form
entries.contrast: Girded is what you will read in American English, almost always in gird your loins or gird for something. Girt has retreated into fixed phrases and nautical description (an island girt by reef). Keep the r in the American vowel — /ɡɝd/, not the British /ɡɜːd/ — and note that the g is hard, as in go.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, elevated in register: bracing yourself for something hard, or belting and encircling in the literal sense.
entries.transitivity: both — intransitive or reflexive in the living sense (retailers gird for the holidays, the mayor girded himself for a fight), transitive in gird your loins and the literal encircling (stone walls had girded the town).
entries.passive: restricted — natural only in the literal encircling sense, and mostly as the short participle: the island is girt by coral, the town was girded by stone walls. No passive of gird for: ✗ the holidays are girded for.

entries.meaning: To let someone use something of yours for a while, expecting it back — and, figuratively, to give a quality to something.
examples: Lend me twenty dollars until Friday.
I lent him my car for the weekend and got it back full of sand.
She has lent that book to at least six people.
The museum had lent the painting to Chicago before the fire.
Banks lend at whatever rate the market will bear.
Credit unions lent less that year than at any point since 2009.
Those curtains lend the room a little warmth.
Her presence lent the event a seriousness it had lacked.
Two new studies have lent weight to the theory.
The novel does not lend itself to a two-hour film.
The basement lent itself perfectly to a workshop.
Come lend a hand with the couch.
He lent a sympathetic ear and said nothing else all evening.

senses.head: Loan something, expecting it back
body: You lend something to someone and they borrow it from you — the two verbs point in opposite directions. Takes two objects with no preposition: lend me a pen. (давать взаймы, одалживать (кому-л.))
examples: Lend me twenty dollars until Friday.
I lent him my car for the weekend and got it back full of sand.
She has lent that book to at least six people.
The museum had lent the painting to Chicago before the fire.

senses.head: Provide money at interest
body: The commercial sense, with a bank or a lender as the subject. Often intransitive: banks stopped lending. (кредитовать, выдавать ссуды)
examples: Banks lend at whatever rate the market will bear.
Credit unions lent less that year than at any point since 2009.

senses.head: Give or add a quality
body: Figurative, with an abstract object: lend weight, lend credence, lend an air of, lend charm. Nothing is returned here. (придавать (оттенок, вес, достоверность))
examples: Those curtains lend the room a little warmth.
Her presence lent the event a seriousness it had lacked.
Two new studies have lent weight to the theory.

senses.head: Lend itself to — be suitable for
body: Reflexive and fixed. The subject is a thing, and the sense is that its nature suits some use. (годиться для, хорошо поддаваться)
examples: The novel does not lend itself to a two-hour film.
The basement lent itself perfectly to a workshop.

senses.head: Lend a hand, lend an ear
body: Two set phrases where nothing is literally loaned: lend a hand is to help, lend an ear is to listen. (помочь, подсобить; выслушать)
examples: Come lend a hand with the couch.
He lent a sympathetic ear and said nothing else all evening.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.third person: lends · -ing form: lending (also a noun: bank lending)
entries.contrast: Lend and borrow point in opposite directions: you lend something to someone, and you borrow it from them. ✗ Can you borrow me a pen? is the classic error — say Can you lend me a pen? The past lent also sounds exactly like Lent, the church season, and it is one letter from bent and sent.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all senses, even the figurative lend weight and lend an ear, where nothing physically changes hands.
entries.transitivity: ditransitive in the core sense — two objects with no preposition (lend me twenty dollars), or one object plus to (she lent the book to a friend). Also plainly transitive in lend weight, and intransitive in the banking sense: banks lend at whatever rate the market will bear.
entries.passive: yes, with either object as subject — the painting had been lent to Chicago, he was lent a car for the weekend. The reflexive lend itself to has no passive: ✗ the novel is lent itself to a two-hour film.

entries.meaning: To spend money or time on the wrong things.
examples: It is easy to misspend a windfall.
The council misspent the entire grant on consultants.
The trustees have misspent money that was meant for scholarships.
He has misspent most of his twenties.
By graduation she felt she had misspent four perfectly good years.
He credits his misspent youth with his skill at pool.

senses.head: Spend money wrongly or wastefully
body: Usually about public or entrusted money, and usually the verdict of an auditor or a critic rather than the spender. (тратить не по назначению, транжирить)
examples: It is easy to misspend a windfall.
The council misspent the entire grant on consultants.
The trustees have misspent money that was meant for scholarships.

senses.head: Misspent youth (waste time or years)
body: You will meet the participle far more often than the base form, nearly always in the fixed phrase a misspent youth — often said with some affection. (растратить впустую (годы, молодость))
examples: He has misspent most of his twenties.
By graduation she felt she had misspent four perfectly good years.
He credits his misspent youth with his skill at pool.

entries.register: rare — prefixed derivative of spend, met almost only as the participle in a misspent youth
entries.contrast: Prefix mis- on spend, so the forms follow spend exactly and need no separate explanation. Two things to watch: the double s — ✗ mispend — and the fact that you will meet the participle far more often than the base form, nearly always in the set phrase a misspent youth.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, the mis- judgment version of spend: money or years put to the wrong use.
entries.transitivity: transitive, object obligatory — misspend a windfall, misspent the entire grant, has misspent most of his twenties. ✗ The council misspent is incomplete.
entries.passive: yes — the entire grant was misspent on consultants, money meant for scholarships has been misspent. In practice you meet the bare participle as an adjective far more often: a misspent youth.

entries.meaning: To spend more money than a rival does.
examples: Big campaigns routinely outspend small ones ten to one.
Her opponent outspent her by two million dollars.
The league has outspent every other sport on television advertising.
Being badly outspent did not seem to hurt her at all.
The startup was outspent from the first quarter on and never caught up.

senses.head: Spend more than a competitor
body: Always takes the rival as its object — she outspent her opponent. Spending past your own budget is overspend, not this verb. (тратить больше (чем соперник), обходить по расходам)
examples: Big campaigns routinely outspend small ones ten to one.
Her opponent outspent her by two million dollars.
The league has outspent every other sport on television advertising.

senses.head: Be outspent (passive)
body: The passive is at least as common as the active, especially in political and business reporting. (уступать по расходам, быть перетраченным соперником)
examples: Being badly outspent did not seem to hurt her at all.
The startup was outspent from the first quarter on and never caught up.

entries.register: neutral to formal — ordinary in campaign and business writing, seldom said out loud
entries.contrast: Prefix out- on spend; the forms match. The trap is the meaning, not the shape. To outspend someone is to spend more than a rival does, and it always takes that rival as its object: she outspent her opponent. Spending past your own budget is overspend — ✗ We outspent our budget should be We overspent our budget.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and comparative: it measures your spending against a rival's.
entries.transitivity: transitive, and the object is obligatory and must be the rival — her opponent outspent her by two million. ✗ We outspent our budget is the wrong verb; that is overspend.
entries.passive: yes, and the passive is at least as common as the active in political and business reporting — the startup was outspent from the first quarter on, being badly outspent did not hurt her.

entries.meaning: To put up more construction than a place needs — or, in engineering, to make something far stronger than it has to be.
examples: Developers overbuild whenever credit gets cheap.
The city badly overbuilt its downtown in the 1980s.
Miami has overbuilt its condo market more than once.
The bridge is famously overbuilt — it could carry twice the design load.
Engineers had overbuilt the frame on purpose, expecting heavier trucks.

senses.head: Build more than a market can absorb
body: The real-estate sense: too many units for the tenants or buyers available. The participle works as an adjective for the place — an overbuilt waterfront. (чрезмерно застраивать, перенасыщать застройкой)
examples: Developers overbuild whenever credit gets cheap.
The city badly overbuilt its downtown in the 1980s.
Miami has overbuilt its condo market more than once.

senses.head: Overbuilt — stronger than necessary
body: An engineering use, almost always the participle as an adjective, and frequently a compliment rather than a complaint. (с избыточным запасом прочности, сделанный с перезапасом)
examples: The bridge is famously overbuilt — it could carry twice the design load.
Engineers had overbuilt the frame on purpose, expecting heavier trucks.

entries.register: rare — a real-estate and engineering term rather than general vocabulary
entries.third person: overbuilds · -ing form: overbuilding (also a noun: decades of overbuilding)
entries.contrast: Prefix over- on build, with the same forms — nothing new to learn. In practice overbuilt works most often as an adjective describing a place with more construction than it can fill: an overbuilt waterfront.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: putting up more construction than a place needs, or engineering something far past the required strength.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive with the place or market as object (the city overbuilt its downtown, Miami has overbuilt its condo market), intransitive with no object at all (developers overbuild whenever credit gets cheap).
entries.passive: yes in the transitive sense — the downtown was badly overbuilt in the 1980s, the frame had been overbuilt on purpose. In the bridge is famously overbuilt the participle has gone adjectival rather than passive.

entries.meaning: To spend more money than you have or planned to spend.
examples: Households overspend every December and regret it in January.
We overspent by four hundred dollars on the kitchen.
The department has overspent its travel budget again.
An overspent budget is easier to explain than an unfinished project.
By the third quarter the agency had overspent every line item.

senses.head: Spend past your own budget
body: Measured against your own limit, which is what separates it from outspend — that one measures you against somebody else. Works with or without an object. (перерасходовать, тратить сверх бюджета)
examples: Households overspend every December and regret it in January.
We overspent by four hundred dollars on the kitchen.
The department has overspent its travel budget again.

senses.head: Overspent — run past its limit
body: The participle as an adjective for a fund, an account, or a line item that has nothing left in it. (перерасходованный, исчерпанный (о бюджете, фонде))
examples: An overspent budget is easier to explain than an unfinished project.
By the third quarter the agency had overspent every line item.

entries.register: neutral to formal — ordinary in budget and finance writing, less common in speech
entries.third person: overspends · -ing form: overspending (also a noun: government overspending)
entries.contrast: Prefix over- on spend, same forms. Keep it apart from outspend: overspend measures you against your own budget, outspend measures you against somebody else. The participle overspent also works as an adjective for a person or a fund that has run past its limit: an overspent account.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, measured against your own budget rather than a rival's (that is outspend).
entries.transitivity: both — the object is optional: we overspent by four hundred dollars and households overspend every December stand alone, while the department has overspent its travel budget takes one.
entries.passive: restricted — grammatical with a budget or line item as subject (every line item had been overspent by the third quarter), but American writing far prefers the participle as an adjective: an overspent budget, an overspent account.

entries.meaning: To build something again after damage or dismantling — a town, an engine, a team, a life.
examples: Volunteers rebuild a few of these houses every summer.
They rebuilt the bridge in eleven months.
By the time we visited, the town had rebuilt almost everything the fire took.
He rebuilds carburetors in his garage on weekends.
The engine was rebuilt twice before the car finally sold.
The team has rebuilt its roster around two rookies.
Ownership chose to rebuild rather than chase a wild card.
It took years to rebuild the trust he threw away in an afternoon.
She rebuilt her life in a town where nobody knew her.

senses.head: Build again after damage
body: The literal sense, typically after a fire, a flood, a storm, or a war. (отстраивать заново, восстанавливать)
examples: Volunteers rebuild a few of these houses every summer.
They rebuilt the bridge in eleven months.
By the time we visited, the town had rebuilt almost everything the fire took.

senses.head: Overhaul a machine
body: Take a mechanism apart and reassemble it with worn parts replaced. Also a noun: the engine needs a rebuild. (перебирать, капитально ремонтировать (двигатель))
examples: He rebuilds carburetors in his garage on weekends.
The engine was rebuilt twice before the car finally sold.

senses.head: Rebuild a team or organization
body: Near-technical in American sports: trade away veterans and start over with young players. Often used with no object at all — the club decided to rebuild. (перестраивать (команду), обновлять состав)
examples: The team has rebuilt its roster around two rookies.
Ownership chose to rebuild rather than chase a wild card.

senses.head: Rebuild trust, confidence, a life
body: Figurative, with an abstract object. The implication is always that something was broken first. (восстанавливать (доверие, репутацию, жизнь))
examples: It took years to rebuild the trust he threw away in an afternoon.
She rebuilt her life in a town where nobody knew her.

entries.register: everyday — ordinary for houses, engines, teams, and trust alike
entries.third person: rebuilds · -ing form: rebuilding (also a noun: the rebuilding effort)
entries.contrast: Prefix re- on build, with identical forms; ✗ rebuilded is as wrong as ✗ builded. One stress note: as a verb the stress falls on the second syllable, /ˌriˈbɪld/, but the noun pulls it forward — the engine needs a total rebuild /ˈribɪld/.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic, always with the implication that something was broken or dismantled first — a town, an engine, a roster, a life.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive in most senses (they rebuilt the bridge, she rebuilt her life), intransitive in the American sports sense with no object at all: ownership chose to rebuild.
entries.passive: yes — the engine was rebuilt twice before the car sold, the town had been rebuilt almost entirely. No passive of the sports sense: ✗ it was rebuilt by ownership does not mean the roster overhaul.

entries.meaning: To tear something violently apart, literally or figuratively. Literary throughout — ordinary American speech uses tear.
examples: High winds rend the sails of any boat left rigged.
The dogs rent the feed sack open and scattered it across the barn.
Frost has rent that ledge into loose slabs.
The scandal has rent the party in two.
By then the treaty had rent the alliance beyond repair.
Grief rends that household every year on the anniversary.
A single scream rent the silence of the church.
Sirens rend the air every night on that block.
The choir sang a heart-rending setting of the psalm.
Her testimony was heart-rending and the room went quiet.

senses.head: Tear violently apart
body: The literal sense, and already elevated in register. Note that the past rent is spelled and said exactly like the ordinary word rent you pay for an apartment. (раздирать, разрывать на части)
examples: High winds rend the sails of any boat left rigged.
The dogs rent the feed sack open and scattered it across the barn.
Frost has rent that ledge into loose slabs.

senses.head: Split a group, divide bitterly
body: Figurative, about parties, families, churches, alliances. This is the sense you are most likely to meet in print. (раскалывать, разрывать (партию, семью))
examples: The scandal has rent the party in two.
By then the treaty had rent the alliance beyond repair.
Grief rends that household every year on the anniversary.

senses.head: Rend the air or the silence
body: Of a sudden loud sound. A fixed literary collocation — a scream, a siren, or a shot rends the air. (разрывать (тишину), оглашать)
examples: A single scream rent the silence of the church.
Sirens rend the air every night on that block.

senses.head: Heart-rending
body: The -ing form in a compound adjective is far more common today than the verb itself, and it is the form most learners will actually meet. (душераздирающий)
examples: The choir sang a heart-rending setting of the psalm.
Her testimony was heart-rending and the room went quiet.

entries.register: rare — literary throughout; ordinary American speech says tear
entries.contrast: The past rent is spelled and pronounced exactly like the everyday word rent — the money you pay for an apartment, and the regular verb rent / rented / rented. Only context separates them: He rented an apartment downtown (paid to use it) versus Grief rent the family in two (tore it apart). Rend itself is literary; in ordinary American speech people say tear.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and violent, literary throughout; ordinary American speech uses tear. Today you meet the -ing form as a compound adjective (heart-rending) more often than the verb.
entries.transitivity: transitive in every documented sense, object obligatory — rend the sails, rent the party in two, a scream rent the silence. ✗ The scandal has rent is incomplete.
entries.passive: restricted — grammatical and occasionally used (the alliance was rent beyond repair, the family was rent in two by grief), but it stays literary; in ordinary prose you would say torn.

entries.meaning: To make something or someone go from one place to another — a letter, a package, a person, a signal — or to knock something suddenly into a new state.
examples: I send my mother a postcard from every trip.
She sent the contract by overnight mail.
They have sent four reminders already this week.
The company sends two engineers to every site visit.
They sent their daughter to school in Vermont.
He has sent the kids to bed early all week.
The gust sent papers flying across the parking lot.
One bad quarter has sent the stock down forty percent.
News like that sends the whole neighborhood to the windows.
Send for the doctor.
They sent for a tow truck and waited two hours in the rain.
The office sends out invoices on the first of the month.
The beacon sent out a pulse every nine seconds.
We have sent out three hundred invitations.
We sent off the application on Monday.
The whole town had sent him off with a parade.
Send in the form before the deadline.
The governor sent in the National Guard.
She sent back the soup twice.
I have sent back everything that didn't fit.
The probe still sends data every eleven hours.
The tower had sent nothing for three days before anyone noticed.

senses.head: Dispatch mail, a message, or goods
body: The everyday sense. Takes two objects with no preposition: send me the file or send the file to me, never ✗ send to me the file. (посылать, отправлять, отсылать)
examples: I send my mother a postcard from every trip.
She sent the contract by overnight mail.
They have sent four reminders already this week.

senses.head: Make a person go somewhere
body: The object is a person, and you have the authority to move them — a child to bed, an employee to a site, a patient to a specialist. (отправлять, посылать (кого-л. куда-л.))
examples: The company sends two engineers to every site visit.
They sent their daughter to school in Vermont.
He has sent the kids to bed early all week.

senses.head: Knock into a sudden state or motion
body: Pattern: send + object + -ing or an adjective phrase. Nothing travels anywhere in particular — the point is the abrupt change. (заставить резко (полететь, взлететь); вызвать (реакцию))
examples: The gust sent papers flying across the parking lot.
One bad quarter has sent the stock down forty percent.
News like that sends the whole neighborhood to the windows.

senses.head: Send for — summon
body: Have someone or something brought to you. The object of for is the thing summoned, not the messenger. (посылать за (кем-л.), вызывать)
examples: Send for the doctor.
They sent for a tow truck and waited two hours in the rain.

senses.head: Send out — distribute or emit
body: Either mass distribution to many recipients, or a source giving off light, heat, or a signal. (рассылать; испускать (сигнал, свет, запах))
examples: The office sends out invoices on the first of the month.
The beacon sent out a pulse every nine seconds.
We have sent out three hundred invitations.

senses.head: Send off — mail away; see someone off
body: Two uses: put something in the mail, or give someone a farewell. In British soccer commentary sent off also means ejected from the game — not an American use. (отсылать, отправлять; провожать)
examples: We sent off the application on Monday.
The whole town had sent him off with a parade.

senses.head: Send in — submit; deploy
body: Submit a form or entry to an organization, or order forces into a place. (подавать, присылать (заявку); вводить (войска))
examples: Send in the form before the deadline.
The governor sent in the National Guard.

senses.head: Send back — return
body: Return something you were given because it is wrong, broken, or unwanted. (возвращать, отсылать обратно)
examples: She sent back the soup twice.
I have sent back everything that didn't fit.

senses.head: Transmit a signal
body: Technical: a transmitter, satellite, sensor, or probe as the subject. The object is data or a signal rather than an object. (передавать (сигнал, данные))
examples: The probe still sends data every eleven hours.
The tower had sent nothing for three days before anyone noticed.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.contrast: Sent is a perfect homophone of cent and scent — three spellings, one sound /sɛnt/, and only spelling tells them apart on the page. There is no ✗ sended. Like lend, send takes two objects with no preposition: send me the file or send the file to me, never ✗ send to me the file.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic in all senses, from mailing a package to a gust that sends papers flying.
entries.transitivity: ditransitive in the core sense — send me the file or send the file to me (never ✗ send to me the file) — and transitive elsewhere, with the object obligatory: ✗ I sent yesterday. The send + object + -ing/adjective pattern adds a complement: sent papers flying.
entries.passive: yes, with either object as subject — four reminders have been sent, their daughter was sent to school in Vermont, the National Guard was sent in. Even the figurative sense passivizes: the stock was sent down forty percent.
entries.phrasal verbs: send away · send away for · send back · send down · send for · send in · send off · send out · send out for · send up

entries.meaning: To pay out money, or to pass a stretch of time — one English verb where Russian splits the job between тратить and проводить.
examples: We spend about a hundred dollars a week on groceries.
She spent nine hundred dollars on a bike she rides twice a year.
The department has spent its entire budget already.
I spent the whole afternoon at the DMV.
She spends every summer in Maine.
He has spent years learning Japanese.
Do not spend your best material in the first ten minutes.
The storm had spent most of its force before landfall.
He has spent whatever goodwill he had left.
Spend the night here if the roads are bad.
We spent the night in the car outside Amarillo.
The plant stores spent fuel rods on site.
A spent match went into the ashtray.
By mile twenty I was completely spent.
The team looked spent in the fourth quarter.

senses.head: Pay out money
body: The core sense, usually with on for the thing bought: spend forty dollars on lunch. (тратить, расходовать (деньги))
examples: We spend about a hundred dollars a week on groceries.
She spent nine hundred dollars on a bike she rides twice a year.
The department has spent its entire budget already.

senses.head: Pass time
body: Same verb, no money involved: spend the afternoon, spend a year, spend time doing something. The complement is usually a bare -ing clause. (проводить (время))
examples: I spent the whole afternoon at the DMV.
She spends every summer in Maine.
He has spent years learning Japanese.

senses.head: Use up energy or resources
body: Figurative: effort, force, ammunition, patience, political capital. The implication is that the supply is finite. (расходовать, тратить (силы, запас))
examples: Do not spend your best material in the first ten minutes.
The storm had spent most of its force before landfall.
He has spent whatever goodwill he had left.

senses.head: Spend the night
body: A fixed everyday phrase for staying somewhere overnight, and the source of the noun a sleepover. (ночевать, оставаться на ночь)
examples: Spend the night here if the roads are bad.
We spent the night in the car outside Amarillo.

senses.head: Spent — used up
body: The participle as an adjective for something with nothing left in it: a spent match, spent fuel, spent shells. (израсходованный, отработанный)
examples: The plant stores spent fuel rods on site.
A spent match went into the ashtray.

senses.head: Spent — exhausted (of a person)
body: Predicate adjective, about people. I'm completely spent is ordinary spoken American English. (обессиленный, выдохшийся)
examples: By mile twenty I was completely spent.
The team looked spent in the fourth quarter.

entries.register: everyday — one of the verbs an American uses without thinking
entries.third person: spends · -ing form: spending (also a noun: consumer spending)
entries.contrast: One English verb covers both money and time — spend fifty dollars, spend the weekend — where Russian splits the job between тратить and проводить. There is no ✗ spended. The participle spent is also an adjective meaning used up or exhausted: a spent match, spent fuel, I'm completely spent.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic for both money and time, and figuratively for using up force or goodwill. The participle spent has become an adjective (a spent match, I'm completely spent), but that is not a linking use of the verb.
entries.transitivity: transitive — the object is normally obligatory (spend a hundred dollars, spend the afternoon, spend the night), though the money object can be left out in economic talk: Americans are spending less.
entries.passive: yes — the entire budget has been spent, most of its force had been spent before landfall. The time sense passivizes naturally too: the whole afternoon was spent at the DMV.

entries.meaning: To straighten something that was bent, or to loosen up and become less formal.
examples: Slowly unbend the paper clip until it is straight.
He unbent the hook, looked at it, and threw it away.
The wire, once unbent, would not hold its shape again.
The old man has unbent a good deal since he retired.
She rarely unbends in front of strangers.
By the end of the evening our guests had unbent enough to laugh at themselves.
He unbent slowly from the garden bed and pressed a hand to his back.
She unbends, wipes her forehead, and goes back to the row.

senses.head: Straighten something bent
body: The literal transitive sense — wire, a hook, a paper clip, a fender. (разгибать, выпрямлять)
examples: Slowly unbend the paper clip until it is straight.
He unbent the hook, looked at it, and threw it away.
The wire, once unbent, would not hold its shape again.

senses.head: Relax, become less formal
body: Figurative and intransitive, about a stiff or reserved person warming up. Watch the -ing form, which pulls the opposite way: an unbending judge is one who will not yield at all. (смягчаться, оттаивать, держаться проще)
examples: The old man has unbent a good deal since he retired.
She rarely unbends in front of strangers.
By the end of the evening our guests had unbent enough to laugh at themselves.

senses.head: Straighten up from a bent position
body: Intransitive and physical: you were bent over and now you are not. Somewhat literary; in speech people say straighten up. (разгибаться, распрямляться)
examples: He unbent slowly from the garden bed and pressed a hand to his back.
She unbends, wipes her forehead, and goes back to the row.

entries.register: rare — prefixed derivative; in speech Americans say straighten out or loosen up
entries.third person: unbends · -ing form: unbending — also an adjective (see Contrast)
entries.contrast: Prefix un- on bend, same forms throughout. The catch is the -ing form, which pulls the other way as an adjective: the verb unbend means to straighten out or to relax, but unbending describes someone who will not bend at all — an unbending judge. Read the word by its job in the sentence, not by its shape.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic: straightening something bent, or a stiff person loosening up. Watch the -ing form, which has gone adjectival in the opposite direction — an unbending judge will not yield at all.
entries.transitivity: both — transitive on physical objects (unbend the paper clip, he unbent the hook), intransitive both figuratively (she rarely unbends in front of strangers) and physically (he unbent from the garden bed).
entries.passive: restricted — grammatical in the physical transitive sense but rare, and the participle usually turns up bare: the wire, once unbent, would not hold its shape. No passive of the relaxing sense: ✗ he was unbent since he retired.

entries.meaning: To make your way somewhere, slowly and by a winding route. Survives almost entirely in the phrase wend one's way.
examples: Every evening the cattle wend their way down to the river.
We wended our way through the crowded market.
By midnight the crowd had wended off toward the parking lots.
The trail wends along the ridge for six miles.
The creek wended through that valley long before the road did.
The bill has wended its way through three committees.

senses.head: Wend one's way — travel, head somewhere
body: The living use of the verb, and it nearly always carries one's way with it. The modern past and participle are wended; went was historically the past of wend but belongs to go now and nowhere else. (держать путь, направляться, брести)
examples: Every evening the cattle wend their way down to the river.
We wended our way through the crowded market.
By midnight the crowd had wended off toward the parking lots.

senses.head: Follow a winding course
body: Of a road, trail, or stream running in curves — and figuratively of something inching through a slow process, as a bill does through a legislature. (виться, извиваться; медленно продвигаться)
examples: The trail wends along the ridge for six miles.
The creek wended through that valley long before the road did.
The bill has wended its way through three committees.

entries.register: archaic — no longer current except in the fossil phrase wend one's way
entries.contrast: This is the one entry in the group you should read twice. The spreadsheet gives the past as went, and that is historically correct — went really was the past of wend. But English handed went over to go centuries ago, and it now belongs there and nowhere else: I went home, and never ✗ I have went. The modern past and participle of wend are wended: we wended our way home. The verb itself survives almost only in that phrase, wend one's way.
entries.verb type: action — dynamic and archaic, alive almost only in the fossil phrase wend one's way; also of a road or stream following a winding course.
entries.transitivity: both — technically transitive in wend one's way, but the object is fixed and reflexive (we wended our way through the market), never free; intransitive of a route: the trail wends along the ridge.
entries.passive: no — the only object is the fixed one's way, which cannot become a subject: ✗ their way was wended through the market. The winding-course sense is intransitive and has no passive at all.
